speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
I feel sure the house will want a report on the situation in India and also on the preliminary action taken by Canada in this regard.
There has been heavy fighting on the northern frontier of India and the Chinese are occupying large areas of Indian territory. We do not, of course, know their ultimate objectives. It is clear that the military situation is serious. As hon. members know, the government of India has expressed its determination to resist aggression. Canada's hope has been that peace could be restored on this troubled frontier on the basis of an equitable and permanent solution. However, in the meantime it is essential that India should be fully supported.
I informed the house last week that the government had been examining, in response to the Indian government's request, ways in which Canada could help. The Indian government has now advised that it is most grateful for the offer which has been made and they are anxious to receive immediately six Dakota aircraft. The government took immediate steps on receipt of this request to have the Royal Canadian Air Force assemble six Dakota aircraft at their repair shop at Trenton and put them into first class condition. These aircraft will be departing from Trenton at noon tomorrow and will be ferried by the R.C.A.F. to India, where they will be turned over to the Indian government.
It is important that India's economic progress and the implementation of her five year plan should not be impaired by the need to defend her frontier, and we shall be mindful of this in considering India's request for military supplies. Other countries have also been approached by India, and we are being kept informed of the constructive steps which are being taken to provide military assistance.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
As already stated, we on this side of the house will support the government in any steps that it is possible to take to assist
India, a nation with which we have built up such very close relations within the commonwealth over the years, as she now finds herself a victim of aggression-though not, presumably, aggression yet in the form of an all out, formal war-by the communist Chinese.
Perhaps the best type of assistance we could give is that mentioned by the Prime Minister, assistance in the way of supplies. India's financial position is not such, we are informed by the Minister of Finance, as to permit payment for those supplies in cash, so we all hope that the terms upon which they are being offered will be as generous as possible to our Indian friends.

Mr. Speaker, I believe we all welcome the words we have just heard from the Prime Minister with regard to direct aid from Canada to our sister nation of India, now so severely put to the test by what amounts to a wide open war with her neighbour to the north. I would assure the Prime Minister that we will give our complete support to any action the government might take toward assisting India at this time.
However, I would just come back to the point, that in standing upon our moral responsibilities at this time we are placing ourselves in the rather peculiar position of probably assisting in the destruction of our creditors as the Indian people face the threat of invasion from the communist Chinese from the north. I think that, in addition to the positive action of which we have now heard, we should be very careful to re-examine our own policies to make sure that we are giving not only practical material support, but also the moral support of knowing that our policies are based upon principles which will carry through to the ultimate moral obligation which is ours in the struggle between communism and the free world.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group will support any action which will assist India in defending her borders. We have that obligation to her as a member of the commonwealth, and as probably the one true hope for democracy in the far east. I was particularly impressed with what the Prime Minister said about assisting in every way to enable India to complete its five year program. If

Canadian Position on Disarmament India is to be an example of the advantages of democratic government in Asia, then she must be assisted in every way possible to raise the standard of living of her people, and I certainly think we in this country could be doing much better than we are doing in terms of the paltry contribution which we are making in foreign aid.
With reference to the suggestion that some form of economic embargo upon China might be considered, I would simply say that we in Canada should ask that this matter be considered by the United Nations. If any form of economic sanctions is to take place, it should not take place on a unilateral basis but rather as part of an international program. We in this group would point out that had China been admitted to the United Nations we might not have the problem of disciplining a country which we have consistently kept out of the world community.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some question was raised on Friday with reference to the attitude taken by Canada in connection with nuclear testing, and in particular with the motion and the several amendments which were before the United Nations. For that reason I feel it proper that I should place before the house at this time something of the stand which the Canadian representatives have taken there in the light of the decision which was made today in the political committee.
The 36-power resolution on nuclear testing, as amended by Canada with subamendments by several other delegations, was adopted by the political committee this morning by the very large vote of 81 in favour, none against, with 25 abstentions. Immediately following the vote on that resolution a separate United States-United Kingdom resolution was also put to a vote and adopted with 50 in favour, including Canada, 12 against, with 42 abstentions. The action which the political committee took this morning on these two resolutions will, I hope, lend new impetus and direction to the negotiations in Geneva which have been marking time while this matter was under discussion in New York.
The purpose of the Canadian amendments to the original 36-power resolution was to attempt to improve it in two respects, first, to link up future discussions with the references to testing contained in the recent

correspondence between President Kennedy and Chairman Khrushchev; and second, to remedy an omission in the original text by incorporating in it a call for an immediate cessation of testing in the three environments-in the atmosphere, under water and in outer space-on which all sides are agreed that no special inspection mechanism is needed.
The subamendment submitted by Ghana had the effect of adding a third element to the Canadian amendments by calling for an interim arrangement during which underground tests would be suspended while the research for a formula for their permanent suspension would be continued. The United States and United Kingdom governments submitted further amendments to the Ghanian proposal to make clear that they wanted adequate assurances for international verification during this interim period. The United States-United Kingdom proposal was accepted, as was that of Ghana, and thereafter the resolution as a whole, incorporating the Canadian amendments thus revised, was adopted with the result that I have already indicated.
Throughout the negotiations, which were complex, Canada has kept in close consultation with all the members of the 18-nation disarmament committee and, of course, with the three other western members of that committee, namely the United States, United Kingdom and Italy. I think we can take satisfaction from the action which the committee has taken, and which will shortly go to the assembly as a whole; for it should provide a constructive basis on which the Geneva talks can move ahead, taking account of the ideas which have been advanced in New York during the current debate. The resolution will also point the way to the method of stopping all tests by January 1, 1963, an element which has hitherto been lacking.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has not been easy, of course, for members to keep up with the deliberations in New York in respect of this extremely important matter because of the changes that have been made to the original 36-power resolution from time to time. However, from what the Prime Minister has said it seems that the original resolution, with amendments submitted by Canada to make it more effective and more practical, along with an amendment submitted by the United Kingdom and the United States to provide for means of verification and inspection-with the inclusion of these new elements into the original resolution and the passing of that resolution by such a large majority in the political committee-is one from which,

as the Prime Minister has said, we can all take great satisfaction. This resolution deals with one of the most important matters before the United Nations and before the world, namely the ending of nuclear tests. As is clear, if we cannot make progress in this dread and practical matter of ending all tests, it is not going to be easy to make the progress which is necessary in other fields of disarmament.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the words we have just heard from the Prime Minister bring a feeling not only of relief but of rejoicing to our hearts and those of all the Canadian people. If any good can come out of the crisis we have just had in Cuba, perhaps this is one point, in that the people of the world have been aroused to an understanding of the closeness of the danger involved in nuclear war. Hence any progress at all which is made in this question toward the ending of nuclear armament is something over which we have just reason to rejoice.
Although the Secretary of State for External Affairs is not present with us today I should just like to take this opportunity to assure him of the complete support of our group in this house in his untiring efforts which he has carried on during these past several years to bring to a successful conclusion that question about which we are now speaking. He as well as freedom loving peoples around the world can be assured that we are concerned, and that we are completely behind him in his efforts to bring about a situation in which we actually can end nuclear testing. This will be the first step toward eliminating nuclear armament and the threat of nuclear war to a world which today certainly is in no position to face up to.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise only to underline on behalf of the New Democratic party members in this house the unanimity of this chamber in congratulating the Canadian delegation at New York for the success it has had in having a proper resolution adopted by the first committee. Like other members of the house I asked questions about this because it seemed to us, as I am sure it seems to every member and as the Leader of the Opposition emphasized, that one of the most regrettable events of recent months was the resumption of tests by the Soviet union followed by the resumption of tests by the United States of America. It is obvious, I think, that until these tests are ended any talk about general disarmament or, indeed, nuclear disarmament is rather empty.
Questions
It is therefore with pride as Canadians that we are pleased on this occasion to join all others in this house in congratulating the government delegation at the United Nations for its work.

Have soils from the Canadian shield area been tested in other areas of Canada for agricultural purposes and, if so, with what results?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Testing of soil from the preCambrian shield area in other areas of Canada, for agricultural purposes, has been limited to the conduct of an experiment at Ottawa over a period of some ten years in which 24 tons of peat was added to sandy soil to determine if this would improve the physical and fertility conditions of the sandy soil. The addition of peat, at the rate of 24 tons per acre, had no effect on the yield of oats and resulted in very minor increases in the yields of potatoes and clover. It has been concluded the addition of 24 tons of peat per acre to improve sandy soils was relatively ineffective and that these soils can be improved more economically from a crop production standpoint by the use of commercial fertilizers, local fertilizers, and the growing of forage or sod crops.
Experience indicates it would not be feasible to transport soil from one area to another to improve conditions for growing most crops.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
1. Interviews in connection
with the labour force survey are * carried out monthly in 165 sampling areas across the country. Of these, 90 sampling areas are cities or urban centres whose population is approximately 15,000 or over. The remaining
Questions
75 sampling areas generally comprise a number of adjoining townships, parishes and the like, including any villages, towns, or cities of 15,000 or less within these boundaries. In each of these 165 sampling areas a carefully determined proportion of households are interviewed each month. In total during any particular survey, approximately 40,000 households are interviewed.
The boundaries of the 90 "city areas" normally coincide with 1951 census boundaries. The boundaries of the 75 "non-city areas" were established by grouping together townships, parishes and census enumeration areas according to industrial composition and character. Maps delineating the sampling areas in use and those not in use, at any point in time, are used to control the areas under enumeration.
The boundaries of the sampling areas were reviewed during 1953 and necessary changes were made on the basis of 1951 census information. At that time, there were 107 sampling areas as compared to 165 at the present time.
Each of the 75 "non-city areas" was selected to represent other areas in the province which were similar with respect to such factors as location, basic industry, percentage of farm households, type of farming, farm income, etc. Each of these 75 areas is therefore, somewhat different in character from the other 74. By interviewing a sample of households within each of these 75 areas, the changing economic conditions in each are effectively represented. Similarly, the sample households interviewed in each of the 90 "city areas" ensures that the changing economic conditions in each of these cities are effectively represented.
2. The boundaries of the sampling areas were reviewed and re-established during 1953, using information from the 1951 census. Sampling ratios were recalculated on the basis of 1951 census population counts. Prior to this time, there had been 107 sampling areas (32 cities of approximately 30,000 population and over, and 75 other areas).
During the period 1953 to the present, the number of sampling areas has been increased from 107 to 165 in order to improve the accuracy of information obtained from the survey. These 58 new sampling areas were generally cities with populations under 30,000 and they were introduced as follows: 5 in 1953, (Charlottetown, Oshawa, Peterborough, Sarnia, Sault Ste. Marie); 3 in 1954, (Rouyn-Noranda, Shawinigan Falls, Chicoutimi); 2 in 1957, (Cornwall, Guelph); 10 in 1958, (Moncton, Galt, Midland-Penetang, North Bay, Orillia, Owen Sound, Pembroke, Stratford, Woodstock, Moose Jaw); 28 in 1959, (Amherst,

Prior to setting up these places as separate sampling areas, they were included as parts of other sampling areas and interviews were, therefore, conducted only in some of them. To the extent that they are now all represented as separate entities, the accuracy of the survey results has been improved.
Of the 75 "non-city areas", which were in the sample during 1953, there have been 41 areas where all households in these areas have been interviewed in subsequent surveys. In order to avoid imposing upon the same households for additional surveys, interviewing has been transferred to other randomly selected areas with similar economic characteristics. These shifts, from one area to another similar area, are called sample rotations and the year in which they are to occur is predetermined by the population within each area. These sample rotations have occurred as follows: 2 in 1955; 4 in 1957; 7 in 1958; 11 in 1959; 6 in 1960; 4 in 1961; 7 in 1962.
These areas comprise groups of townships, parishes, villages and towns. Their boundaries can only be defined by reference to master maps maintained at the dominion bureau of statistics.
3.(a) There are now approximately 755 enumerators used each month in connection with the labour force survey. This figure varies slightly from month to month, since there are always a few enumerators who are unable to work because of illness or other personal reasons. Under these circumstances enumerator assignments are adjusted so that households are not omitted from the survey.
(b)	Enumerators engaged for this survey may be male or female. They must demonstrate aptitude for interview work and be capable of understanding and following detailed instructions. They must be personably suitable, courteous, reliable and of good character.
(c)	Enumerator candidates are interviewed by a fully qualified member of the permanent regional office staff. A written test is given to determine clerical aptitude, comprehension and ability to follow detailed instructions. They are further assessed with respect to related experience and personal suitability.

If found suitable on all counts a contract is then signed stipulating rates of pay, allowable expenses and other conditions of work. The enumerator then takes the oath of secrecy as prescribed under the Statistics Act.
(d)	All enumerators work on a part time basis. Normally an enumerator's assignment involves 4 or 5 days work during a prescribed week of each month.
(e)	At the outset enumerators are paid at the rate of $1.45 per hour. After 2 years of satisfactory work an enumerator's rate of pay may be raised upon recommendation to $1.60 per hour. A mileage allowance of 9 cents per mile is paid when travel by automobile is required. Upon occasion other expenses are paid in accordance with government travel regulations.
4.	Prior to November 1952, the labour force survey was conducted only once every 3 months in the months of March, June, August and November. speechtext: What Is the approximate number of farmers in the counties of Restigouche and Madawaska, New Brunswick, and what was their average income for the years 1957, 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: RESTIGOUCHE AND MADAWASKA COUNTIES, N.B.   INCOME OF FARMERS
speechtext:
The number of farms counted in the 1961 census of agriculture in Restigouche county (New Brunswick) was 508 and in Madawaska county 858. It is not known how many of these farms are operated by full time farmers. It is possible that some of them are operated by persons whose main occupations are other than agriculture. The 1961 census also indicates that, of the 508 farms in Restigouche county, 200 were commercial farms-that is, farms from which the sales of agricultural products, including forest products from farms in a 12-month period, were $1,200 or more. Similarly, in Madawaska county, 388 farms were commercial farms as defined by the census in 1961.
Income from farming operations published quarterly by the dominion bureau of statistics is only available for the province as a whole. The census of agriculture for 1961 will have estimates of gross sales of agricultural products, by county, but these tables will not be ready for publication until mid-1963.

Inquiries of the Ministry broadcasting of these programs until further notice. The board pointed out that it could not undertake any action without the opportunity to study such evidence as was available. I am told that information is now being provided to the board.

speechtext: You amaze me.

Mr. Speaker, the reason for this so-called austerity emergency program which was introduced on June 24, just after the election, was the financial and exchange crisis which we were facing at that time and, indeed, had been facing for weeks before that time. We got into that crisis because the government had let the situation get out of hand over the weeks and the months preceding the acceleration of the crisis, which took place in the third week in June. We do not have before us all the statistical information which we have requested dealing with the developing dollar crisis.
We have not yet received the return showing the forward transactions of the Bank of Canada. Even, Mr. Speaker, if and when we get that information, the statistical information itself will not be able to tell the whole story.
However, we now have enough. The figures we have received are such as to confirm absolutely the fact that pressure on the Canadian dollar was very serious from the time of the last budget of April 10. Indeed, prior to that time, from January 1 to the budget of April 10, there had been a drop in our exchange reserves during that period of $385 million. That drop should have been a cause for anxiety. Hence the trouble had begun even before the budget was introduced into this house. It was a trouble which owed its origin to the policies preceding that budget and indeed going back for many months.
The trouble began to increase right at the beginning of the year. However, in April, after the introduction of the budget, it built up to a crisis. From April 10 to May 4, on the basis of the figures which have been given to the house, our exchange reserves dropped in that period of about three weeks-it was less than a month-by $200 million. In one day, from April 30 to May 1, they dropped by $39 million. That drop brought about the forced devaluation-it was not planned but was forced-of our dollar in the midst of an election campaign.
The government, of course, tried to pretend that this devaluation was a great master stroke of policy that had been carefully planned. Ministers talked as though the decline in our dollar reserve-at least they talked that way during the election campaign -did not matter very much, and as if it was just exchanging one kind of dollar for another. As we have been so often reminded in this house, the Minister of Agriculture even suggested that, in so far as he and some of his


colleagues were concerned, the only trouble with devaluation was that the dose had not been big enough.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that after May 2 and devaluation our reserves increased and the position strengthened somewhat. I think they increased in a few days by $14 million. We recall the explanation for that increase at that time given by the then minister of finance. The explanation was that there had been-what shall I call it-a windfall of 62 millions of dollars and I quote his own words, "from special transactions not associated with the open market".
However that improvement may have been brought about, Mr. Speaker, it was only temporary. Devaluation gave only a breathing spell, a temporary relief. Pressure on the dollar built up again after devaluation, and any chance of restoring confidence at that time was certainly destroyed by the Minister of Agriculture who gave the impression, "Well, the dollar is going down again shortly because the cabinet is divided on this matter". The run on the dollar then built up again and pressure became great again. Yet on May 28 the Minister of Finance said, and I quote, that the Canadian dollar was a "good, sound, stable currency; one of the strongest in the world."
That was on May 28. What happened, Mr. Speaker? Let us consider the five days from June 11 until June 15. On June 12 we lost $35 million. On June 13 we lost $20 million. In two days therefore, Mr. Speaker, we lost $55 million. That was in two days before the Prime Minister's broadcast of June 14 which gave a very rosy picture indeed of the situation of the country and which stated that nothing in regard to the situation was concealed from the Canadian people.
There has been a controversy over these statistics, over the figures and their meaning. One way in which this controversy can be settled is by referring this matter to the standing committee on banking and commerce and allowing that committee, with the evidence before it and witnesses to be summoned, to go into this whole question. We will then find who was right and who was wrong.
It is, of course, true that after June 18, with the accelerated run on our dollar, the government had no alternative but to replenish its foreign exchange reserves which it had treated so lightly and had guarded so carelessly; and it replenished them, I admit, in the only way possible at that time, namely by borrowing from foreign banks and by arranging stand-by credits. No responsible person denied at the time the necessity of

that procedure and I do not think any responsible person would deny it now, faced with the desperate situation into which the government had got itself and the country.
However, what else was needed? Long range action was needed, Mr. Speaker, to get at the causes of our trouble as the only way to permanently restore confidence in the Canadian dollar. The Prime Minister and members of the government more than once since that time have emphasized that this was just a temporary emergency program, and that long range policies would be brought in and long range steps would be taken to permanently restore confidence in our dollar and to strengthen the economy generally. We have been in session now in this house for a good many weeks and we had eight days or nine days of debate on the economic state of the nation. However, none of those long range programs have been brought in.
They are not even ready.

Moreover, there is no indication that they are ready to be brought in. Of course the basic cause of our difficulty leading up to this crisis from the beginning of the year has been the slowdown of our economic growth, causing unemployment, and massive chronic budget deficits leading the government into financial irresponsibility, producing unproductive expedients, with changes of mind and weak action along with strong words; instead of a constructive policy to bring forth more production and more jobs in this country. However, we did not get from the government these constructive long range policies. We got words, expedients and half measures. The program that was brought in, the temporary emergency program which is still with us, is a program of restriction. Today I am dealing only with two of its main features, namely tariff surcharges and tight money.
The tariff surcharges represent an increase in taxation of about $200 million a year. Those are the figures which we have received. That amount is now being collected-an amount of approximately $200 million a year-from the people of Canada and the only authority for the imposition and the collection of that taxation has been an order in council passed by the government under legislative authority which can be and has been challenged. Whatever may be the facts about that situation, there is no doubt there is no argument over the fact that we in this House of Commons are not to be permitted to pass judgment on this taxation of $200 million which was levied by the government by order in council.
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
It is an extraordinary thing that this taxation was levied by the government, in accordance with the method I have just mentioned, very shortly indeed after government spokesmen had boasted in the election campaign that they had lowered taxes. They had not in fact done so. In total the people were paying more taxes before this emergency taxation than when this government came into office, but government spokesmen used some carefully selected figures to boast about reducing some taxes. Yet a week after the election they raised taxes by some $200 million, did so by order in council under legislative authority the legality of which is at least arguable, and then refused to let parliament decide whether or not this extra taxation was justified.
When that was complained about the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) pointed out that once you give the government a vote of confidence on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, by doing that you confirm everything the government has done before that time. That is an extraordinary constitutional position to take, and I commend to my friends in the group to my left this position, that by giving the government a vote of confidence on the speech from the throne they were supporting, confirming and approving everything that had been done in respect of this emergency program since June 24.
Not only did the government raise taxes in this way by these surcharges, but they raised the kind of tax which can be the most unfair of all the taxes that we pay. They raised taxes by tariff increases. That kind of taxation hits the ordinary person more than any other kind. That is the kind of taxation that hits every housewife when she goes into a store, taxation that hurts most those who can least afford the extra burden. Yet the government have done this and are keeping these extra taxes in force at a time when they say everything is fine with the economy, we are in the midst of a great upsurge, there is nothing to worry about, yet at a time when the prices that Canadians have to pay to live are at a record high.
What a contrast between talk and action once again. What a contrast also with the new kind of talk that the government has recently started, and I welcome its beginning, about trade conferences, about joining with the United States, the common market and other NATO countries in order to lower tariffs and remove as far as possible all obstacles and obstructions to trade.
Higher tariffs and surcharges only intensify one of the basic causes of our economic troubles. But under this government Canada had been standing aside from the main stream

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money of economic co-operation among the free nations. Indeed, until very recently we have been on the sidelines growling while Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States are launching new, imaginative and farsighted trade policies. They are looking to more trade, to lower barriers, while this government is raising obstructions to trade through surcharges which, even though justified in an emergency by the government's own reasoning, surely cannot be kept on when, as they say, the emergency is now over and everything is fine.
Of course I know the minister is going to tell me, when he gets up to take part in this debate, that these surcharges are only temporary. That has been continually stated by the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet. They are only temporary; they are going to be removed at the first possible opportunity. But if the revised budget estimates which the Minister of Finance brought in two weeks ago mean anything, the government's intention must be to continue this extra taxation at least until March 31, 1963, because he included it in his revenue estimates.
What is he going to do after March 31 next? What about the manufacturers who want to know now whether they must base their plans for the future on the existence of these higher tariffs, these surcharges? How are they supposed to know what to do? How can you expect the economy of this country to run smoothly when it is exposed to the uncertainty that the government itself creates? What is the government's policy in this matter? The country certainly has a right to know. Businessmen have a right to know. Workers have a right to know. Housewives have a right to know. Is it to be lower tariffs, or is it to be higher tariffs indefinitely by means of these surcharges? Are these surcharges to be temporary only, or are they to be permanently temporary like some of the wartime buildings in Ottawa that are still called temporary buildings and in which so many people still work today? I say, Mr. Speaker, that these surcharges should be dropped now. If the government is not going to do that it has a duty to say what it will do, how long it plans to maintain this extra taxation, and then ask parliament to decide in regard to that policy.
There is another aspect of the emergency program, and only one other, to which I wish to refer, and that is tight money, high cost money, expensive money, high interest rates, money which it is difficult for people to get who need the money to expand their business activities. The Minister of Finance in his jovial way said the other night that we did not have such tight money but he was not quite sure what it is. Perhaps he will tell us

this afternoon what he means by tight money, and explain to us what he means when he says we have not got it. We have the same story with regard to tight money that we have with regard to surcharges, with regard to government words as contrasted to government action. In the election campaign the government boasted that it had ended tight money. It ended, said the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) on May 17, and said the Prime Minister on May 26, "when we ended Mr. Coyne". Apparently that was what was supposed to be involved in the shameful Coyne affair. That was their excuse. They were putting an end to tight money and they had to get rid of Mr. Coyne in order to get rid of tight money at the same time.
Yet within a week after the election they raised interest rates. They told the Bank of Canada to do exactly what they said in the election campaign they had stopped the bank from doing. When the election campaign began the bank interest rate was 3J per cent. After the election it was raised to 6 per cent, almost twice as high, Even now after some gratifying reductions it is 5 per cent. What we have had since June is the highest cost money that this country has ever known, with all the restrictive results that are bound to come from that situation in terms of business expansion. Never since we have had a central bank has its interest rate been as high as during this period.
What does tight money as I have defined it do in a situation of excess unemployment, inadequate growth and idle productive capacity? Its one merit, and I do not deny this merit, in the situation in which we found ourselves at the end of June is that it temporarily lessens exchange problems largely by encouraging the inflow of money. Of course, a great deal of the inflow in these circumstances is bound to be and has been hot money. But that in itself involves a long term liability as payment for a short term advantage. It exposes us to more exchange trouble when the hot money decides to cool off and go elsewhere. Second, tight money hurts small businesses which particularly depend on bank credit. It discourages industrial growth. It is a very blunt instrument indeed, particularly handicapping those areas most in need of special development. Three, it especially hurts the construction industry, which also needs a lot of bank financing of a comparatively risky kind, and which is so very important in the provision of jobs. Four, it encourages businesses of all kinds to put off investments and new developments in the hope that credit will become cheaper and more plentiful later. Five, in all these ways

tight money means fewer jobs and more unemployment. Six, tight money particularly handicaps Canadian companies in competition with United States controlled companies which can go to their parents across the line for financial help which they find difficult in obtaining in this country. In that effect, tight money policies of the kind I have indicated are not only discriminatory in respect of regions in this country, which are usually most prosperous, but this policy discriminates in favour of satellite companies or subsidiaries of United States companies against Canadian owned companies.
Seven, tight money raises the financing costs of municipalities and other public authorities, even the federal authority. When the Minister of Finance was giving his revised budget he had to add no less than $40 million to his predecessor's estimates for this year's service of the public debt. Tight money, therefore, means higher costs and higher taxes at all levels of government. Finally, in order to escape this as far as they can, the bigger municipalities and other public bodies are driven to do part of their borrowing abroad. This means more interest payments and capital repayments to foreigners in the future. In other words we are mortgaging our future. This intensifies rather than lessens our long term problem of the balance of payments.
The balance of payments problem has been serious, I know, over many years, years before this government came into office. In the early weeks of this year we were told it was gradually being eliminated, that everything was improving. We know now, on the basis of the figures for the first seven months of this year, that the balance of payments problem is going to be as serious as it ever has been, including an unfavourable balance in our trade commodities.
These, then are some consequences of tight money. Yet the Minister of Finance gaily pretends he does not really know what tight money means, but he is sure we have not got it. Well, Mr. Speaker, tight money is what we have got today, high cost money, high interest rate money that is hard to get for the person by whom money is required for expansion, production and jobs. The consequences of this kind of tight money are exactly the opposite of what this country needs today.
Oh, there have been lots of occasions in the history of our country in the last 10 or 15 years when a tight money policy could be justified. I refer to times of booming expansion when it was absolutely essential to prevent runaway inflation, we did not have idle capacity, we did not have massive unemployment. But we are not in that situation
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money today, so we must relate a tight money policy to the economic situation in which we find ourselves.
Today we need expansion, not restriction. We need to encourage industrial growth, not make it more difficult. We need more construction work for municipalities at lower costs in local taxes, not less construction and higher costs. We need to encourage Canadian ownership of our own industry. But, as I have said, tight money makes it easier than ever for foreign companies to buy out Canadian companies. We need a plan for a reduction of our balance of payments deficits on a steady, long term basis, instead of adopting expedients which worsen our problems in the future.
The policies we need, Mr. Speaker, are quite contrary to tight money policies and to higher tariff surcharge policies. They are policies of more capital for industry, more capital for municipalities. They are policies to encourage the growth of industry to create more jobs, to restore confidence in our economic progress, to raise production and income and so bring back stability to the nation's finances. Those are the measures we need, the measures that my colleague and I have put forward and will continue to put forward in this house on behalf of the Liberal party. Those are the policies which the next government of this country will act upon.
So, Mr. Speaker, I believe, and I know a great many members of this house believe, that tight money and tariff surcharges are the very opposite of a cure for the problems which we have in Canada today. The government does not want to talk about it, but the amendment which I am about to put forward now will give every member of this house a chance to express his views in favour of tight money and tariff surcharges, on the policy of the government, for or against tight money and tariff surcharges. The division will show where we stand on this matter. There could hardly be, Mr. Speaker, very much doubt about where the members of the Liberal party stand on this matter. I suppose there could not be very much doubt about where the members of the Social Credit party should stand on this matter.
I recall that immediately after the austerity emergency program was put into effect the Canadian Press were consulting the leaders, deputy leaders and co-leaders of the various parties as to their attitude toward these policies. According to the Canadian Press the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said in Rouyn that Mr. Diefenbaker was proposing two absolutely contradictory solutions to Canada's financial problems. He said,

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money referring to the emergency austerity program, that Mr. Diefenbaker ought to resign rather than make proposals like this. Well, Mr. Speaker, our amendment this afternoon condemns those proposals, and we are going to give all members of this house an opportunity to support us in this condemnation.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money, introduced on June 24 this year, should be stopped at once.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me as I have been listening to the prelude to this amendment which has just been placed before the house, that in my opinion it is a question of the pot calling the kettle black.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A pretty big pot.

As I have said before, in so far as finding an alternative to the present economic situation is concerned, all the Liberals have proposed is more of what we have had before. The leader of the official opposition sings one song today. When he was a member of the Liberal government in 1956 he sang another song, and he was in exactly the same position then as this government finds itself in today-
Oh, come.

-in a question of tight money and higher interest rates. It is rather interesting to note that in a series of four or five newspaper clippings which I have here, we find him today completely reversing the stand he took a few years ago. For example, on February 12, 1956, in the Ottawa Citizen we find an article written by Douglas Leiterman of the Southam news services talking about the tight money policy of the Liberal government being the cause of the national housing program sagging. We jump across to the Vancouver Province of November 10 of that year and find the Liberal government being condemned severely for a tight money program that has put agriculture in a very difficult situation, and we find the Liberal government were supporting and were directly responsible for that tight money program. Here again a great Liberal newspaper, the Toronto Star of October 27, the same year, devotes a major editorial to the tight money problems that arose under the Liberals. We could go on to a number of other editorials and newspaper comments, but it would take too long to deal with them now.
Go ahead.

It seems to me that the hon. members in the Liberal section of the house are more determined to upset and wreck the economy of this country at this particular time, and so place themselves in what they think will be a position of political advantage, than they are concerned with doing what is good for the country. Members of that party have in the last few weeks travelled around the country and accused myself and the members of our party of being guilty of supporting the Conservative government. To tell the truth, all we have been trying to do is save the country from the wreckage the Liberal party would try to bring about. I say again-* in this respect I agree with the leader of the official opposition-that if what the government says is true, we do not need an election; and if what they say is true, we cannot afford to have one at this time. This is the obvious motive behind the amendment with which we are faced today. It is not a question of trying to ease the tight money program or better the position we are in at this time.
I was very interested to note, in turning back to Hansard, that the leader of official opposition on October 19 not only assured hon. members of this house but also the Canadian people at large that if the subamendment that was proposed in the speech from the throne was defeated, they would give their support to this parliament in trying to bring forward some constructive legislation for the good of the country. In fact, when I-
There is none.

There isn't any simply because hon. members on this side of the house have talked so much and at such length on the very legislation they have said they agreed with, and there has not been time to bring in legislation.
The record does not prove that.

This is what the hon. member had to say:
When I spoke in the debate on the address on October 1 X indicated that if the house should reject the motion of want of confidence being put forward at that time, as well as subsequent similar motions moved during that debate, this would mean that the government would have a mandate at least to introduce its legislative and other proposals. I also indicated at that time, and I repeat it now, that each of those proposals would be considered on its merits by the official opposition in exactly the same way as if the government had a clear majority in this house. That did not mean then, and it does not mean now, that we were, or are, giving approval in advance to any measure or action taken by the government. It did mean we would give each measure objective consideration in the light of the public interest.
I suppose, then, that the-

In this particular situation, however, what is the motive behind this amendment? I would ask the leader of the official opposition to think this through a little bit. Do you want to add chaos to the confusion which we agree the country is in at the present time? Do you want to project us into a situation where we face an election simply because you want to further your own political ends? This is something we must consider. Where would we have been in the last week, in the face of the crisis we have been through, if we had been in the midst of an election campaign? I can well imagine that the hon. members who are determined to bring this thing to a crisis, obviously, through the amendment that has been made, would enjoy an election campaign over the Christmas holiday. I am sure it would season up the festivities of the celebration which is so near at this time.
I think the real issue here at the present time is simply this. Are we, sitting in this house of minorities as we are, going to give the government an opportunity to meet their present obligations and go ahead and bring in some legislation that we need, or are we going to plunge ourselves into an election campaign? As far as we over here are concerned-and we say this for the good of the country and not for any political expediency-
Oh, oh.
You are afraid of one.
-an election at this time would be wrong for Canada.
Why?
I think it might even-
It will be wrong for Social Credit.

-be wrong for the civil servants who, through the very nature of this supply motion, might have some chance of getting their pay by Christmas, which otherwise we are trying to deny them. However, leaving that as it may be, Mr. Speaker, I think the situation we find ourselves in requires from us some positive thinking and some positive action. I would hope that in this House of Commons we will get through 27507-3-82
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money this particular supply motion which is necessary for the government to have passed, in order that we can have the opportunity of judging them according to the legislation which they must later bring down.
In that regard I have a few constructive suggestions to make. I would suggest to the government that it is necessary immediately to take steps which will correct the situation we are in at the present time. We heard the other day that in their economy measures the government have cut out a great deal of the money that was previously allocated to the Colombo plan. The reduction in the amount of Canada's current contribution to the Colombo plan as a means of further reducing the budget deficit is, surely, a gesture of gross national selfishness or callousness, particularly when applied to a fellow nation of the commonwealth such as India at a time when she finds herself in such a difficult position. I hope the government will see fit immediately not only to restore the aid which has been passed on to India for many years but also to increase it in respect of her basic food requirements, if not in any other way. We were glad to note today, however, that some constructive action is being taken to help India in other ways as well.
In approaching this over-all problem as other problems, I do not think our primary motive should be one of debating. I am not interested in debating at this time. The taxpayers of Canada have been paying for providing a debating society in our parliament for too long, and what we heard today as a preliminary to the amendment being moved is the same as we heard a few weeks ago and a few weeks before that. It is time we got down to business and settle some of the grave questions facing us, rather than trying to display to the public and to the press our ability to outwit each other verbally.
We have come to a crossroads in the affairs of this nation. We have to decide now, not next year or the year after that, whether we are going to remain Canadians or whether we intend to throw in the towel and become the fifty first state of the U.S.A. In this regard, never before has our economy been so invaded, backed by the power of the press, radio, television and finance, as it is at this time. Given this picture, it is necessary for the government to take action to release the pressure on the tight money program we have now.
So you vote for it.

I find it is very interesting; we get applauded from both sides of the house. Yes, but not according to the procedure

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money and not according to the devious means which the movers of this amendment are following at the present time.
Let the people decide.

The most important thing at the present time is for us to understand that legislating in piecemeal fashion to correct some small anomaly in the economy here, or some case of injustice there, will never meet our needs. The side effects of this type of legislation can be appalling. Our need is to decide on the fundamental direction of our economy and to adapt all economic policy to it. In this way we avoid-in Stephen Leacock's phrase-rushing madly off in all directions.
The principle that the government should take action to improve the working of the economic system is well established, and it is one with which all parties agree. How this should be done is a matter of dispute. Let us take as a concrete example the raising of capital, whether it be capital for industry, capital to finance the government's deficits or capital for essential public works. We live in a free enterprise economy. We should, therefore, expect to find that capital for commercial purposes would be raised on the open market. Instead, what do we find? We find a fantastic increase over the past four years in the activities of the industrial development bank which now has more than four times as many branches and three times the number of customers as it did only four years ago. In addition, it makes loans at more than twice the rate it did four years ago. We were told when the industrial development bank came into being that it was a bank of last resort intended to provide capital for risk projects when private investment was not ready to provide it. Instead, it has widened its scope. Where does the money come from for this lending? By far the greater amount of it comes off the printing presses of the Bank of Canada. Originally, the I.D.B. was designed to fill gaps in the lending structure of the nation-to make credit available where none was available before commercially. Now it makes loans in direct competition with existing commercial sources. Because it has Bank of Canada money available to it at government borrowing rates it can without exception undercut any competition there may be in that field from normal sources. The end result of this must be a completely state controlled pattern of investment-a negation of our private enterprise system.
But in other fields, the reverse is true. Suppose a government, federal, provincial or

municipal, wishes to carry out non-commercial improvement for the good of the community, one would naturally expect it to go to the Bank of Canada or to its agent, the industrial development bank, and by exchanging its promise to pay for the promissory notes of the bank, receive money to pay for the improvement more or less at cost. Is this what happens? Oh, no. Governments borrow on the commercial market, thus automatically doubling the cost of every long term project they undertake; they have to pay as much for the financing as they do for the project itself. Moreover, the very fact that they do this is precisely the reason that commercial risk capital is so scarce and hard to come by, the situation which tends to make necessary institutions such as the industrial development bank.
Let us settle one matter of principle at this point. In a private enterprise economy, commercial risk capital should come from private investors. Equally, government social capital should come as low cost credit from the Bank of Canada, provided inflation would not be increased to an excessive extent by doing so.
We have no scarcity of raw materials in this country. Heaven knows, we also have no scarcity of unemployed. Suppose we did set up a municipal development bank. The industrial development bank would be able to return to its role of supplying special commercial credit as needed, while the municipal development bank would provide the capital which our social needs require. Employment would receive the stimulation which is required at this time and we would see our economy begin to move forward. What, in fact, would we be likely to see? One hundred million dollars could go to the Atlantic region for projects such as the Chignecto canal and the Montreal turnpike, for the improvement of harbours and fishing facilities. Spend this every year for some years and think of the transformation that would take place in this region, the facilities it would have, the commercial development that would take place. And remember, the resources that this money would put to work are there already, idle.
