Mr. Speaker, one of the greatest needs we have in our country today is for the freeing of our credit restrictions through making municipal or public capital available according to our ability to expand and produce. It would solve many of our unemployment problems and it would put that necessary stimulus into our economy which, if it could be accompanied with the necessary tax reform which we need today, would put us on the road to recovery. Thus I believe that in our long range program these are things about which we should be talking.
Along with this we are very concerned about the high interest rates which are developing at the present time, and I believe they relate directly to the problem we have of restrictive taxation. I think the iniquitous and destructive tax system which we in Canada have cannot wait for, say, the two years which are usually necessary for a royal commission to bring out their findings. If we can combine our public needs for capital in the ways I have suggested and free the restrictions which limit our own investment capital, which we have in abundance-we lack only the confidence to use it-and then combine them with a realistic tax reform program, now, we could move forward in this country to a great era of prosperity. These are not just my words or the thinking of a few of us here in this comer of the house, because I do not believe that there is any hon. member in this house or any collective group of members who themselves know all the answers to the problems which we face today. In this regard I am convinced that in this house of minorities, at least for a while, during this emergency we ought to be working together to deal with some of these problems in such a way that the country as a whole will benefit.
In regard to my suggestion for tax reform, let me quote from the Financial Post in its latest editions, where it has written about this very problem. In an editorial which is headed: "Let's get moving on tax incentives", in the edition of August 18, I find this:
A tax system that discourages effort, which penalizes risk-taking and which makes it more profitable for a lot of people not to be enterprising and not to create new jobs, surely makes poor sense in today's Canada.
A little later it says:
Who will make the jobs necessary for renewed progress? Plainly, it won't be Canada's weak and discouraged manufacturing industry-unless there are new tax incentives designed to speed industrial growth.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
In the same paper on October 27 I find an editorial headed "Real tax reform can't wait", and here I quote words spoken by A. J. Little, a partner in the accounting firm of Clarkson, Gordon and the immediate past chairman of the Canadian tax foundation, when speaking to the Canadian club in Toronto. He said:
"With intelligent and forthright action Canada should be out of the woods in three years. I suggest we need more tax incentives applied now, the promise of a corporate tax rate reduction in one year's time, an indication of a further corporate tax rate reduction and a personal tax rate reduction in two years' time, and removal of the tax incentives in three years' time."
Then he went on to say:
"Surely it would be good common sense to take every step possible to encourage the development and growth of small and medium private business and encourage retention in Canada, and yet with our tax structure we do just the opposite."
The hard truth is that lassitude, indifference and ignorance of the basic tax changes so urgently needed apparently persist in the exalted places where policy is made-
I am sure I do not know what place he is referring to there.
-and the result is the perpetuation of an outdated tax system that discourages initiative, destroys capital and militates vigorously against growth in production and employment.
For instance: Canada, as a country where the health and development of secondary industry is so urgent, stands in desperate need of more investment capital. Yet our estate tax laws, which produce only a dribble of national revenue, make it almost impossible for family or closely held corporations to survive, let alone expand over the generations.
Between punitive estate taxes and vicious rules concerning "designated surplus" Canadian companies are terribly handicapped.
This editorial clearly outlines, and states in a practical way, some of the changes which should be brought about now in our tax reform system. Therefore, it is our opinion on this side of the house that instead of trying to force the crisis this time upon parliament and upon the Canadian people, we should permit this supply motion to pass and that we should demand from the government that they bring in the necessary financial and economic reform now. It could be done, as I have mentioned, very simply in making more public or social capital available. It could be done through tax reform, which would encourage the capital that we already have to be put to work, and then we could have some hope at least that of coming out of this winter and there would be less danger of crisis than there is at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, we should like to move a subamendment to the amendment already moved in light of the remarks I have made. Therefore I should like, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Mar-coux), to move the following subamendment:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following at the end thereof: "and replaced

with a policy of debt-free money and constructive proposals to foster balanced domestic economy and balanced international trade".
Mr. Speaker, there are just a few remarks I should like to make in addition to those I have already made in referring to the subamendment in its latter wording. In this question of bringing our economy back to the position in which it should be, in which we can get going forward at a rate of expansion of at least 5 per cent or 8 per cent of our gross national product per year, it is absolutely essential that we consider the matter of world trade. In this regard it is not good enough that we talk about a world trade conference in a year or a year and a half. It is necessary at this time that we take the leadership and do something about solving our trade problems now facing us. I have mentioned this matter previously and I again suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it would be an ideal time to take steps toward the bringing about of a commonwealth trade conference.
If Britain is so tied up with her intentions to join the European common market at this time, I think that Canada should take the lead and try to bring this about. We already have a commonwealth economic committee, one which could be very easily charged with the responsibility of doing the preparatory work that such a trade conference requires. I am convinced that the other commonwealth countries, in view of the problems they themselves face in the same regard, would be only too willing to co-operate. If we did this, along with the working out of freer trade patterns within the commonwealth, we could also be talking about the need of some kind of new arrangement for commonwealth settlements. One of the problems facing us today is this question of settlements as far as international trade is concerned. I have in my hand a copy of a speech made by the chancellor of the exchequer of the United Kingdom, namely Right Hon. Reginald Maudling, member of parliament and member of the cabinet in Great Britain, who makes some very interesting remarks in this regard. He states:
I believe it is universally accepted that a growing volume of world trade calls in the long run for a growing volume of liquidity, even if not necessarily in arithmetic proportion ...
There are those who argue for a return to the classical gold standard. 1 find it difficult to accept this proposition. Either it means that the volume of world trade must be tied to the amount of gold that can be mined and acquired by monetary authorities, which seems to me a proposition that is not intellectually sustainable, or the volume of gold available must be brought in line with world reserve requirements by variations in the price of gold, and the difficulties of this course are only too clear to all of us ...
At present gold is supplemented by the two reserve currencies-the dollar and the pound

sterling. But there is a fundamental difficulty about this system, namely that the reserve currencies are short term liabilities of the United States and the United Kingdom-one nation's reserves is another nation's debt.
Mr. Maudling goes on to state as follows:
The gold exchange system has already undergone extensive development in the last 17 years, particularly in the much wider use of the dollar. But despite the many advantages of the system as we know it today, I cannot believe that its evolution can stop here, or that we already have the final answer to the longer term problems. We shall have to be prepared to supplement present international payments arrangements if we are to make certain that they do not act as a brake upon the possible expansion of world trade and production.
Then he goes on to say this:
Some people have seen in the obligations created under the borrowing scheme the germ of a truly international paper which might in due time become acceptable and transferable between the monetary authorities and so become a familiar holding among reserve assets. It would certainly be worth while to explore this possibility. I am myself, moreover, attracted by the thought that we might develop a system of co-operation between the leading trading countries in the form of a mutual currency account in the fund.
Herein I see a real suggestion that could take its germ beginning in the commonwealth and which could be later expanded to meet the needs of all the nations of the west as we look towards free trade patterns on the world scene. In this regard here in Canada I believe that it is our opportunity to take a lead in this. I believe that we should take steps to initiate a commonwealth trade conference. I should also like to see a commonwealth ministers of finance conference where the various ministers of finance would get together in order to work out these very problems. I think it is a positive suggestion in this regard to see that we set up-and we have had need of it for a long time-an export-import bank that would permit us to take the beginning steps relating to this need of expanding world trade. I would remind hon. members of this house-and I am sure we all appreciate it in some sense at least-that the greatest threat today to the world's peace is the threat of hunger. We find that many of our scientists and our international economists are speaking about this very thing. To quote one of the great United States scientists today, "The world's greatest need is hunger". Then on the other hand I pick up a copy of the Western Producer dated October 25, 1962, and there I find an editorial under this heading, "Food is our most potent weapon". Through trade facilities such as those I can see here, I believe it will be possible for us to turn our production loose in this country, particularly agricultural production and through proper trading channels and proper trading facilities, make these goods available
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money to the peoples of the world who need them at this time. This is the pattern of constructive thinking that I think we ought to be taking. Therefore, we on this side of the house, or shall I say in this corner of the house, as certainly I do not believe the thinking follows through with the members on my right, move this subamendment. We move this subamendment to the amendment with the thought that herein lies the essential basic policy that can correct the situations which today weigh upon us and hinder us from going forward economically and taking our part as we should as a progressive nation reaching forward into a new era of development, which could be so if only our financial and economic policies would permit us to do so.

Mr. Speaker, may I say that you will have no difficulty with regard to correcting me about reading from a prepared text since I have no prepared text and it is probably just as well that I have not any. My position might be as the old man said about the new minister, "You read it and did not read it very well, and it was not worth reading". It is therefore probably just as well that I have not a prepared speech to deal with what I think is one of the most important questions to come before this parliament.
In moving this subamendment to the motion to go into supply the leader of the Social Credit group said something about motives. I for one am not in a position to discuss the motives of the Leader of the Opposition.
You would be out of order if you did so.

I can speak only about my own motives in dealing with this matter. Prior to parliament being convened I and my colleagues took the position that we were not going to support a motion of no confidence in the government just for the fun of bringing the government down, that in our opinion we ought to hear what the government had to say, see what legislation it proposed to place before the house and make our decision in the light of what would be in the best interests of the people of Canada.
When we come to the question of the austerity emergency program we are not dealing with it on a partisan or political basis. We are not opposed to this program merely because it gives us the opportunity to vote no confidence in the government. We deal with this program on the basis that it vitally affects the lives of the Canadian people and because it will vitally affect the life of our economy in the months and years ahead.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
Ever since the government announced the austerity emergency program on June 24 I and the group with which I am associated have taken the position that irrespective of what may have been the motives in bringing forth this program it could not have been better calculated to do the opposite of what was needed if someone had been deliberately drafting it for that purpose. Here is a program that consists mainly of three parts, tariff surcharges, reduced government expenditures and tight money and high interest rates. I submit that all three of these measures, by the simplest laws of economics, are bound to increase unemployment rather than cure it; are bound to result in contraction of the economy rather than expansion of the economy; that tariff surcharges are bound to raise the cost of living particularly on those items which are brought into Canada; that this takes part of the purchasing power which people would use for other goods to pay for the increased cost of living; that the result of reducing government expenditures, whether in capital programs or in social capital, means particularly the destruction of job opportunities which might have materialized. Finally, a tight money program can have no other effect than to reduce the capacity of municipalities and provincial governments, small businessmen and corporations, to carry out the programs which they had intended to initiate had they been able to borrow money at low and reasonable rates of interest.
In a situation such as we had in 1961, when the growth in our gross national product was less than our population growth and when our unemployment figure was some 7 per cent of our labour force, we contend that this was not the time to reduce government expenditures. This was the time to increase them. This was not a time to introduce a policy of tight money but a period to introduce a policy of easy money and low interest rates so as to stimulate the economy and provide full employment.
I want to be just as fair as I possibly can and I say at once that certainly the situation in Canada has improved since 1961. In the first nine months of this year there has been an upswing and this should be readily acknowledged. Certainly I speak for our group when I say that we hope it will continue. But this upswing, it should be remembered, is in comparison with the trough of 1961, the low point in the business cycle. This upswing was due to two factors which I suggest are not likely to continue for very long. The first factor was the effect of the devaluation of the dollar which made it possible for us to increase our exports to foreign countries. I suggest that the beneficial effects of that devaluation are not likely to continue

very much longer as exporters increase their prices. The second reason for the stimulus in the early part of this year was the large government expenditures which were up some 4 per cent, but they are now being cut back so that we cannot expect to get any benefit from that.
Therefore I suggest that the government's emergency austerity program should be completely reversed. I was impressed with the fact that the Leader of the Opposition in moving his amendment simply suggested that the emergency austerity program of tariff surcharges and tight money should be stopped at once. I would have appreciated it, as I am sure other hon. members would, if the Leader of the Opposition had told us what they would put in its place, what constructive measures the official opposition would propose when we stop this emergency austerity program. If the official opposition expects to be the government, I submit to them most respectfully that the people of Canada have a right to know what they intend to put In place of the austerity emergency program which they are asking to be discontinued.
In the limited time I have I want to deal with only one aspect of the kind of program which we in this corner of the house would like to see introduced in place of the austerity program. We are convinced that too little recognition has been given to the fact that the real problem in Canada today is not a lack of production or a lack of capital investment. I am constantly amazed at the references made from time to time to the fact that we must have more capital when as a matter of fact it can be shown that during the past four years very substantial quantities of reserve capital have been built up by corporations in this country, and have not been reinvested. Figures for the first nine months of this year show that, although profits were up 3 per cent, expenditures for capital equipment by corporations increased almost not at all. In other words, these corporations do not lack capital. They do not need additional capital at this time. They are not even using to the full the productive capacity they have. The real reason for the lack of demand for capital is the lack of effective consumer demand. We in this corner of the house are suggesting that the emphasis of a fiscal and monetary policy at this time should be directed toward increasing effective consumer demand on the part of the Canadian people.
We suggest that this can be done in three ways. First of all, it can be done by increased government expenditures in those fields or those segments of our economy which are underdeveloped. It can be done, first of all, by

increased expenditures by the federal government itself. I need not enumerate the scores of things which need to be done, for example, such as a second trans-Canada highway; national power grid; improvements of harbour and shipping facilities, increased research in a score of fields; national parks. The federal government itself could put money into the pockets of consumers of this country by engaging in large scale public works and, above all, by a tremendously accelerated housing program for low income groups.
Some gentlemen suggest that there has been quite a housing program, and there has been a good housing program in the main for people of middle and upper income groups. This country has not even begun to tackle in a serious manner the problem of housing for low income groups, for old age pensioners and people of that type. In almost every country in the western world today, subsidized housing has become an accepted fact for people in low income groups. We could also make money available to the municipalities in the form of social capital for schools, for hospitals, for streets, for sewers, for water facilities, recreation facilities and libraries.
I am always interested in noticing how quickly people reverse their position. From 1945 until 1961, I attended every federal-provincial conference and appealed to both Liberal prime ministers and Conservative prime ministers to activate the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act under which money can be lent to municipalities at a 2 per cent interest rate to enable them to carry on their necessary programs. I always got support from the Conservatives when they were in opposition. Now, I have no doubt I could get support from the Liberals since they are in opposition. I want to tell the house, Mr. Speaker, that of the scores of municipal councils I have met in the last three or four months, every one of them has told me the same story. They were not in a position to carry on the kind of programs that they envisaged this fall and winter unless they were able to get social capital at low rates of interest from some other source than the open market to which they must go at the present time. The same thing is true of the provincial governments.
The provincial governments would undertake large scale programs for senior citizens' housing, for the improvement of provincial parks, for increased road building, if they could borrow money at low rates of interest. I am suggesting that this provision of social capital would put people to work, would put money into circulation, would stimulate effective demand, would do more than any single thing to help get our economy moving.
Tariff Surcharges arid Tight Money
I want to suggest that the second front from which we should tackle this problem of increasing consumer demand is to take immediate steps to lower the tax burden on middle and lower income groups. Most economists agree that there is a close relationship between the level of income and the propensity to consume. Almost all of us know that people in the upper income bracket save a larger percentage of any increase in their disposable income than do the people in the lower income group, who naturally have to spend almost every increase in their disposable income because of the demands of their families and because they are always living close to the border line. It would be possible to put into the pockets of hundreds of thousands of low income and middle groups in Canada increased purchasing power by making the necessary adjustments in the Income Tax Act when the budget is brought down.
There has been a good deal of talk in recent years by economists as to what this affluent society of ours means in Canada and the United States. Hon. members will recall that J. K. Galbraith did a study of this in the United States. The figures for Canada are not available beyond 1959, but they are rather interesting. We find that in that year Canada had a labour force of 6,228,000 people, of whom 1,985,510 or almost two million, some 30 per cent, did not even earn enough to be charged for income tax purposes. This means that almost two million income earners did not earn $1,000 a year if they were single or $2,000 a year if they were married and without any children.
These income tax figures show that the top 5 per cent of our taxpayers received 17 per cent of the total income before taxes and the lower 5 per cent received 1.5 per cent of the total income before taxes. Let us see how taxes have redistributed the national income. After taxes, the top 5 per cent received 15 per cent of the total income and the lower 5 per cent after taxes received slightly better than 1.5 per cent of the total income. In other words, the top 5 per cent received ten times as much as the bottom 5 per cent. The top 25 per cent of the taxpayers earned over 43 per cent of the total income after taxes and the bottom 25 per cent received less than 12 per cent the total income after taxes. About 15.5 per cent of the taxpayers earned less than $2,000 and 36.5 per cent earned less than $3,000. Only 1 per cent earned over $15,000 and they represented 6 per cent of the total income after they had paid their taxes.
I suggest, therefore, that we are deluding ourselves if we do not recognize that there is

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money still wide inequality in the distribution ol income. If we merely give everybody $100 a month or $100 a week, whatever it may be, that will not get to the people who need it. If we are going to put purchasing power into the pockets of the people who need it, we must do it through the income tax mechanism by setting a minimum standard that people require in order to live, and making that exempt for income tax purposes.
The third front on which we need to tackle this problem of increasing consumer purchasing power is by stepping up our whole program of security payments, old age pensions, veterans pensions, family allowances, all forms of health insurance, and so on. All these payments represent a means by which we redistribute income. There are hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who live on very little more than the pensions which they get. This does not enable them to buy very much in the way of consumer goods. By increasing social security payments we would tremendously increase the demand for consumer goods on the part of this very substantial sector of our economy. Today men like Galbraith in the United States and Professor Titmus in England have pretty well established to the satisfaction of most economists that an expanding economy is almost completely dependent upon an adequate system of social security. The old days are gone, when people can condemn the welfare state. Today we recognize that the welfare state in some form is not only demanded by virtue of social justice but is also essential to provide the necessary purchasing power for an expanding and growing economy.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that if we had the three things which I have suggested would increase purchasing power-namely increased government expenditures in the field of social capital, an adjustment of income tax so as to lessen the burden on those in lower and middle income brackets, and substantially increased social security payments-this will inevitably mean we will have a deficit budget. I want to say that we in this group are completely opposed to those who think there is some virtue in a balanced budget by itself. We certainly take strong opposition to those who hold that view, including, may I say to my Liberal friends, Liberal newspapers such as the Winnipeg Free Press, who seem to be convinced that an expanding economy will somehow be brought about if only we balance the budget. Thirty years ago the myth of the balanced budget was destroyed once and for all by John Maynard Keynes, who pointed out to the economists of his day what has since been accepted by most economists throughout the world, namely that there is nothing sacred about 12 months, any more 

than 20 months or 60 months, for balancing a budget. Keynes said that what we ought to be thinking about is balancing the budget on the business cycle, and whether or not we balance a budget or whether we have a surplus or a deficit should depend on what stage we are at in the business cycle; and that if we are in, as we are now in Canada, a period when the economy is sluggish, when there is a lack of economic growth-as there has been for five years-when there is unemployment, this is the time to spend money; this is the time to increase the money supply.
What have we been doing? In the months of July and August we decreased the money supply by over $500 million. This is the time to increase government expenditure. As Keynes pointed out, governments do not lose by increasing their expenditure; they put people to work; they increase production; this increases their tax revenue and the next year they can spend more money. Then he said that when the time comes, as it will, when you have full production and full employment and there is a danger of inflation, the government reverses its technique and takes out of circulation, by way of taxes and other means, more money than it spends. So the government may balance a budget over a period of years in conformity with the business cycle, but not just because 12 months is the time to balance the books.
As has been pointed out again and again in this corner, almost every country in the western world today is following the policies and principles of Keynes in carrying out cyclical budgeting techniques. Britain has not balanced a budget in the last 12 years; France has not balanced a budget for ten years; Sweden has balanced her budget only once in the last ten years; Germany has not balanced her budget for the last seven years. These countries are not going broke; they are growing and expanding at rates of 4, 5, 6 and 7 per cent. These countries have unemployment rates of less than 2| per cent, because they have recognized that there is nothing sacrosanct about balancing a budget every 12 months.
I submit to the government that they were not elected to balance the budget. They were elected to get our economy going, to promote economic growth and to provide jobs for every able bodied person in Canada. That is the kind of job I think the people of Canada expect them to carry out. Some will say, if this is so, why has the government tried to balance the budget? They did not balance the budget in the past. It was not deliberate deficit balancing in the last few years; it was deficit financing by mistake; it was deficit financing that

came as a result of over estimating the economic growth and thinking it was going to be 7 per cent, and it turned out to be less than 2 per cent. Why are they now suddenly deciding that they must balance the budget? I submit that the reason the government has adopted this policy is this; they have been compelled to do so as a consequence of pegging the Canadian dollar at 92| cents in relation to the United States dollar.
We in this group have taken strong exception to pegging the dollar. We have argued that had the government taken expansionary monetary policies, increased growth and production, this would have been more effective than pegging the dollar. We maintain that by pegging the dollar the government is now having to use resources to bolster its international reserves which ought to be going to promoting economic growth and providing jobs. We think this is a mistake. We believe that a floating exchange rate would permit this country to pursue full employment policies at home without aggravating our balance of payments problem abroad. Indeed, the balance of payments problem might be alleviated, because full employment causes unit costs of production in Canada to fall.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the things we would suggest as an immediate program for promoting economic growth and providing full employment. We recognize that these are immediate steps. The long term answer, of course, is much more fundamental. The long term answer, we believe, lies in planning the economy of this country, in mobilizing our financial, material and human resources, so as to put idle men to work on idle resources, so as to make use of all the idle funds we have in Canada to increase our wealth production, to provide jobs for all our people who are able to work. There was a time when talking about democratic economic planning was immediately put down as being just a cranky idea of socialist doctrinaires. The fact is that today democratic economic planning has been accepted by almost every country in the western world, starting in Sweden 31 years ago under the leadership of Gunnar Myrdal and now covers almost every country in Europe and many in the rest of the world. The country which has made most progress in this field is France. Last year I had the privilege of reading the verbatim report of the conference between the French economic planners and the British civil servants who were being groomed to set up a planning agency in Great Britain. That agency has since been set up; it is known as the economic planning council. It is interesting to see what France, 27507-3-83
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money West Germany, Holland and Italy have done by planning their economies.
The fact is, we have always had some planning and we are going to have more planning. The only thing which it is important for us to decide is: who is going to do the planning and for whom? As corporations grow larger, as economic power becomes concentrated in fewer and fewer hands, planning is either going to be done by small groups of directors responsible to nobody but themselves or it is going to be done by the government of this country responsible to parliament and to the people of Canada. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the day is past when the man in the street any longer believes that what is good for General Motors is necessarily good for Canada. There is a growing recognition, as Professor Keirstead was reported as saying the other day in one of the Toronto newspapers, that planning by gigantic corporations is planning for their profit. The time has come when we must have planning in the public interest.
We in this group will not be satisfied to see only what the amendment suggests-that the austerity program should be stopped at once. We should like to see in its place a program designed to increase effective consumer demand, to put idle people to work, to begin generating capital resources to get this economy moving. I believe this government never had a greater opportunity and that no government in the history of Canada ever had a greater opportunity. The people of Canada are prepared to follow leadership, if that leadership shows it has a sense of purpose and a sense of direction. If this government were prepared even at this late hour to set up social and economic goals and then mobilize the resources of this country toward the attainment of those goals they would get the support of the people of this country. Certainly, they would get the support of the members of this group. So far we have not seen any indication that the government has any such intention. We have seen nothing which would convince us that the government intends to reverse its program and, instead of constricting the economy with tight money, a high cost of living, and reduced national expenditures, launch upon a program of expansion and development.
I want to say a word to my Liberal friends, and tell them I am disappointed. While I agree with their criticism of the auterity program, I had hoped we would get from their spokesmen-we may do so before the day is over-a constructive alternative program to the austerity program. It is significant, for instance, that they have suggested that two features of the austerity

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money program be stopped-surcharge tariffs and tight money. But they say nothing about government expenditures. Does this mean that the Liberal party also is worshipping at the throne of a balanced budget? I think we have the right to know. Let me say, in closing, as far as the Liberal party is concerned, that neither their conduct during the 22 years they were in office nor the program which they have presented so far would give me any reason to feel they would be likely to do any better if the people of Canada were to put them on the treasury benches.
I hope the government will make use of this debate to tell the house what they propose to do. I hope they will not simply regale us with statistics of the improvement we have made during the last six or eight months. I suggest this is not the answer. I suggest the momentum we have had from the devaluation of the dollar will not carry us far through 1963 and that the curtailment of government expenditure is going to have an adverse effect during the next six months. I urge the government to reverse its program while there is still time and to give this country the kind of national leadership it needs, the kind it deserves, and the kind to which I am convinced it would gallantly respond.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the applause. I must confess I had hoped it would continue for a little longer in order to give me a greater opportunity to review the notes I have in front of me as well as to shorten the time in which I have to speak before six o'clock.
However, I shall be speaking now until six o'clock, and before dealing directly with the subject before us I should like to express my personal satisfaction at being able to follow the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam, the leader of the New Democratic party. I think I came to this house, some years ago now, after the hon. member had left it, possibly for greener fields. We are very happy to have him here today. If it is necessary to have representatives of the New Democratic party-and apparently it is thought so in some places-we are fortunate that it should be the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I am glad, as I say, to have the opportunity of speaking after him. If I do not attempt to answer all the questions he has raised it is not because I do not consider them worthy of attention but because there will be other speakers in this debate who will undoubtedly deal with some of them.
Perhaps I could also take this opportunity to comment on the statement that our old friend the hon. member for Kootenay West
[Mr. Douglas.)
is retiring from the position of house leader of the New Democratic party. Some of us have sat in this house with the hon. member for Kootenay West for many years. We have not always agreed with everything he has said, but usually he took such a broadminded view that it was possible to agree with him in part, at least. He is a member of this house whom we are all proud to call our friend, and since he has been relieved of some of the responsibility he has been carrying I presume he will look younger while his associates will look older. I wish him the very best of everything.
Now to refer to the amendment which has been brought before the house today. There are many matters which can be raised in connection with it, but not having the opportunity of knowing, nor should I know, what the amendment would be about, I am not in a position to deal with it concretely, as perhaps one would be if one were bringing in an amendment oneself. However, there are some comments I should like to make about it. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said it was based on the fact that it would have been better for the economy of this country to dispense immediately with what he called the austerity measures, and he pointed specifically to the surcharges and to what he called tight money. I will refer to tight money again in a moment or two, because I am not clear yet what the Leader of the Opposition has in mind when he talks of tight money. At one moment I thought he was talking about interest rates, then at another moment about the quantity.
Both.

speechtext: He says he is talking about both.
I did not say anything, but that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
However, I would point this out. Of course, before my hon. friend got down to the wording of his resolution he sort of waffled around over the picture as to who was responsible for what, who had done the developing, and all the rest of it; but he did admit, as I think everybody admits, that there was an economic crisis in June following the run on the exchange fund. He also admitted that some drastic steps were necessary. I think he went so far as to say that under the circumstances the government probably took the best steps they could. As a matter of fact, it has been said in some very responsible economic journals, Mr. Speaker, that the government took a series of prompt and courageous steps which controlled the run on the dollar and largely corrected the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I say this: I am informed, as we all know from reading that this is not the first country which has had a run on its exchange funds. We also know that this is not the first country which has an economic problem at this time. We know that many countries have gone through these problems, and it may be the fact that there are still other countries, either the same ones or others, which will have to go through the same experience. In every case the country going through that problem or crisis was compelled to take certain emergency measures, measures which were to rectify the situation, and over a period of years or months, or whatever it may have been, went a long way toward that rectification. But I am told, Mr. Speaker, and from what I have read I believe, that no country, in such a short time as from June to November-from the time the economic crisis developed and the exchange crisis developed in this country until today-has been able, or was asked, or was expected, to take away the steps which have been taken to deal with their economic problems. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, with firmness and with respect to my hon. friend, that I think it is an attitude of absolute political irresponsibility to suggest, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) pointed out a moment ago, without any suggestion of an alternative, that tonight, with an axe, like chopping off a rooster's head, we do away with the economic steps which have been taken by the government and which have gone so far to rectify the situation with which we are faced.
The other part of the resolution deals with the surcharges, and the fact that they should be immediately repealed. As has been stated in reply to a question on orders of the day, I think today, and as the hon. member knows, these matters are now being considered again by representatives of all the countries sitting round a table and discussing this problem of surcharges, and the changes which the government proposes to make and the action it proposes to take. Again I say that a speech such as we heard from the Leader of the Opposition when dealing with the surcharges, at the very moment when these matters are being discussed at an international gathering in Geneva, is an act far removed from political responsibility and does no good service to Canada but rather hurts the government and the country in dealing with the situation. Again I say it is an act of political irresponsibility.
Mr. Speaker, why is this resolution brought forward at this time? Because this question is of such importance, such dominating influence on the public thinking of this nation, that the opposition party has to raise it 27507-3-83J
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money today? I have here, simply by a strange coincidence, Mr. Speaker, the daily Gleaner, a paper published in Fredericton, the edition of November 3, which is Saturday last.
It is a good Tory paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not so sure about that.
It supports the Tory party blindly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then it follows the blindness of the Liberal party, because it started to publish the Gallup polls. It started to publish them in its first edition. It was put in red, and thereafter they have published it twice weekly. The first question of the poll concerns the austerity plan. I am not sure what this mysterious word "austerity" includes, but I am sure that some of the factors that the Leader of the Opposition mentioned are included in the word "austerity". The first question asked was: "Have you heard or read anything about what has been called the government's austerity program?" Mr. Speaker, do you know that over the national scene on a national survey 56 per cent of the people had heard about it and 44 per cent had not heard about it at all? Yet, when it comes to the problem of the drug thalidomide, which concerned the house a little while ago, some 96 per cent of the people in Canada had heard of that. So I doubt that this austerity program was of such pressing importance that it needed to be brought up at this moment, and this emergency action that the Leader of the Opposition has suggested taken.
The second question in this Gallup poll was: "In general, do you approve or disapprove of the program?" Over the national scene, 52 per cent of the people said that they approved of it, 27 per cent said they disapproved, and 21 per cent said that they had no opinion because they had not heard of it. So that is the survey as far as the national scene is concerned dealing with this austerity program at the moment.
Then we are also told, and this is repeated and repeated and repeated, that something must be done about these measures because they will add to the cost of living; that this devaluation is going to add tremendously to the cost of living. We have devalued our dollar for a period of a great many months. It started in at a premium and has gradually come down and come down, until now it is down to $0.92J. I have here the most recent figures for the cost of living index in the United States, where they have had no devaluation, and therefore have not been faced with this awful spectre of increasing prices such as my hon. friends shiver about.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money In the United States the cost of living has gone up 2.2 per cent, whereas in Canada, according to recent figures, it has gone up 1.8 per cent. So it is 1.8 per cent as compared to 2.2 per cent. Therefore, I think I can deny emphatically that devaluation, these surcharges, or any other of the steps taken by this government, have materially affected in any way the price index in Canada. Of course there is no question that certain prices will go up; that is obvious. If you import oranges, or grapefruit, or a Cadillac car, or other products, some luxuries, some necessities, the cost will go up; but as I have pointed out, the increase has been relatively minor according to these figures.

Mr. Speaker, would the minister permit a question? Would he tell the house what period is covered by these figures for the cost of living increase in the United States and Canada? 1 mean the 2.2 per cent and the 1.8 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was from the beginning *of last year. I gave other figures the other day when speaking on the first motion dealing with the cost of living increase over a period of 15 months. However, this index is computed on a slightly different basis. We hear a great deal about the fact that something must be done about the lagging economy which is threatened by these austerity steps which we have taken. In the speech here the other night in opening the debate on the fiscal and financial problems of the country I stated that the increase in the gross national product would this year be 7 per cent, one of the highest in all of our history. I still stand by that prophecy or that statement. I do not think it will be refuted by events as they develop, barring some unforeseen catastrophe. Again I say there is no authenticity for these dire prophecies.
I am always intrigued by people who say, "Oh, you are doing very well now, we have to admit that; but think how low you were last year and you are only coming up out of the trough. In a few months you are going to be down in the trough again and then you are going to be worse off than ever". There have never been so many dire prophecies of doom by people facing these facts and these figures. Their only explanation is, "You were down in the trough; you are going up, it is true and as far as we are concerned-they say this under their breath-we hope you do not go up forever, but you may; but next year you are going to come down." Perhaps we shall come down. It is fair to make an assumption, Mr. Speaker. I am willing to admit that we have had a very rapid growth during this year or this period. However, I also say


that the policy which we have inaugurated-I refer to the policy which my predecessor started and which I am trying to carry on, namely the policy of economic expansion- will I believe continue to develop the economic growth of this country and we shall not be facing the dire disaster which is so often prophesied for us.
A moment ago I think my friend said that he thought the effect of the devaluation would soon be lost to us and that we would soon have rising costs. He referred to rising costs and all the problems of exports and imports and costs of production which would result in our loss of the advantage of devaluation. That is a prophecy. I am not prepared to deal with prophecies, Mr. Speaker. All I know is this, that I have met a great many Canadian businessmen and industrialists of repute and certainly not all of them by any manner of means were supporters of this party. I refer to the party of which I am a member. A great majority of them have said that we have not yet begun to feel the full effect of devaluation in a positive sense and that in another six months the economy of this country will be developing and growing much more rapidly than it has developed and grown in the last six months. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am prepared to accept those prophecies rather than the prophecies we hear from time to time with regard to the dire disaster that faces us.
That is because they expect the Liberals to be in power in six months.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the last word in doom and gloom.
That would certainly end the progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I come back to the first line of the resolution which is before us with regard to tight money. As I said, I am intrigued to know exactly what is meant by tight money. I understood the Leader of the Opposition to interject a moment ago that he meant both interest rates and supply of money. You can have tight money, Mr. Speaker. I think there have been quite a few of us in this building or in this chamber who sometimes experienced tight money when perhaps interest rates were not too high and when perhaps it was in fairly good supply. I wonder how many members here in this house and who have been here for any length of time have not had a score of constituents come to them and tell them that money is awfully tight, that they could not borrow from the bank and that if that member would only endorse a note for $50 they could go to

the bank and get $50. The fact that they endorsed a note does not increase the supply of money in whatever bank it might be presented. However, it might have increased the possible creditworthiness of the constituent, if the member was unfortunately caught to such an extent that he was obliged to endorse a note. Some of them developed the practice of endorsing the note and then telephoning the bank manager before the constituent could get back and telling him to be sure to turn the note down anyway. However, there were all sorts of situations such as that.
Individuals, of course, through hardship, through misfortune, sometimes through their own fault and sometimes without it whatsoever, through circumstances absolutely beyond their control, have found it difficult to get money or to get credit. One can appreciate that situation and sympathize with it. One can also, sitting on the government benches, appreciate the fact that it is a very good amendment for the opposition to move. It is always nice to be able to say, "You know, you should have more money", the inference being that "If we were only there, there would be more money for you and it would be much easier to get". You can appeal to a large number of individuals perhaps politically on an argument such as that. However, I suggest that it is not a very politically responsible one at this time, and in the circumstances in which we find ourselves.
There is no question that there was an emergency. There is no question that we have come out of it very well. There is no question either that we still need to continue and to maintain certain protective steps in order to guarantee our situation.
A moment or two ago my hon. friend-and the first thing I know I shall be debating with him rather than with the Leader of the Opposition-came out, as I recall it, in favour of a floating rate and said it was a terrible mistake to peg the dollar.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hear "hear, hear" from over there on the opposition side. I am not going to debate the merits of pegging the dollar or of a floating rate. Not long ago I happened to be in a position-it was a couple of weeks ago-of meeting a group of businessmen, including two of Canada's leading bankers. One of them got me off in a room and told me that it was the act of an imbecile to peg the rate. An hour later another banker of equal prominence got hold of me and said, "Did so and so talk to you about that?" He said, "It is an act of imbecility if you did not peg the rate". Hence when you get leading bankers debating
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money the matter in that way, I am not going to debate the merits of it at this time.

May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would point this out to the hon. gentleman. From what he said I gathered first that if we did not have a pegged rate it would not be necessary to use any of our dollars whatsoever in the exchange fund and that we could sit with it floating up and down like a cork in the rapids. I might suggest to him that whatever the merits of the one system or the other, you would still need to have dollars in the exchange fund and you might need a substantial number of dollars in it, whether the rate was a floating one or a pegged one.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
The minister says he is not going to deal with the question whether we should have a pegged dollar.
At this time.

Yes, at this time. My hon. friend, for whom we have the greatest admiration, is nevertheless the Minister of Finance. Does he not think that at this time he ought to take the opportunity to tell the house and the country what his view on this question is, as Minister of Finance, at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in telling my hon. friend what my view is and what the view of this government is on this matter, and surely my hon. friend knows it. I knew he was going to ask this question and I thought it was a good opportunity to take a thirty second breather. I was hoping he would take two and a half minutes to ask the question, as he usually does, instead of one minute. The intention of the Minister of Finance and of this government is to maintain the Canadian dollar at the pegged rate where it is now. That is its policy and it is going to be continued. Without indulging in a debate but for a moment adverting to the remarks made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam -and I said I was not going to go into the merits of what he said-I just point that out to him, and I think everybody in the house knows it. Certainly that is our policy on that matter, and there can be no question whatever.
What about this matter of the level of money or the supply of money and the interest rate? As I said, I am not sure whether the Leader of the Opposition wishes to make his position more clear on that matter when he

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money comes to deal with the tight money policy, whether he was referring to the bank rate or whether he was referring to the money supply, or whether he was referring to both. I think at one stage he said it was the highest rate since Canada had a central bank.
I would ask the minister to tell us what he means by tight money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am asking the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman moved an amendment here in this house, this afternoon, and submitted it to this parliament, deploring the austerity measures. He referred particularly and specifically to tight money but as far as I know he did not enlarge on that in any way, shape or form. He simply used the term "tight money" which, as I said, makes a great appeal to everyone who has been refused a loan by a bank. It could get votes from a certain number but I think it will also lose the votes of a lot of responsible people who would like to see it more clearly defined and who would regret this approach being made at this time, when we are facing the situation that we are facing.
I have tables here, Mr. Speaker, which have been sent to me, dealing with the quantity of money or the money that is available, and I think it is only right that I should put some of these figures on the record. I have them going back over a period of years and I am going to put a few of them on the record at this point before six o'clock. Tight money, of course, must be tied in with bank loans. If bank loans are decreasing then there would naturally be some evidence of tight money, but if bank loans are increasing substantially there would be some suggestion that money was not so tight. I want to tell the house that from June, 1961, to June, 1962 general bank loans increased on an average of $88 million a month.
What about 1956?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am coming to those figures too. I have got them. It is true that after the crisis hit us at the end of June there was a levelling off in August, a decrease in general bank loans, but despite the levelling off in August the increase between the end of June and the end of September averaged approximately $90 million a month. Do hon. members opposite call that tight money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Liberals were not creditworthy.
The first joke in six months.
You are always telling jokes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You have a standing joke over there in the member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is my impression that the Minister of Finance has the floor. Hon. members may wonder when they read Hansard whether this has been a round-table conference.
Ask the Minister of Justice to be quiet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Someone a moment ago asked me about 1956. I have the figures here on a per capita basis. I hope no one will suggest that I have done this to mislead the house in any way because they are figures that were sent to me. I can change them into some other unit if the house wants that done. In June of 1956 the publicly held money supply was $685 per head for the whole population. In June of 1957, one year later, and this is rather significant in the light of history, it was $676 per head. In other words, the supply of money had decreased slightly between June, 1956 and June, 1957.
I am going to give the figure for September, 1962, and I am using September because it is the last month for which I have a record.
I was criticized the other night for having used one month in one year and another month in a second year but I used the month in the second year that was the last one for which we had figures available. That was the only reason I did so.
As I said, in 1957 when we came into office the money supply was $676 a head. In September, 1962, the month before last, it was $783 a head, an increase of over $100 a head during the period. That is rather significant, Mr. Speaker, when you apply it to the nation as a whole.
Talking about tight money again in so far as the banks are concerned, I will give the figures on a per capita basis now and the general figures later. General bank loans in Canada in June, 1956, amounted to $256 a head. In June of 1957 they had gone down $5 to $251, but in September of this year they were $355 a head or a little bit over $100 a head more across the board than at the time we came into office. In view of that very sketchy but I believe absolutely accurate record of the financial picture, if this government can be accused of tight money then I say that we do not know what is meant, and that is why I asked the Leader of the Opposition just what he meant by tight money.
We also have the lending by various government organizations. Between September 30, 1961 and September 30, 1962 industrial development bank loans increased in number from 1,364 to 2,085 and in amount from $71 million to $92 million. In the fiscal year ended September 30, 1957, at the time when this government came into power and inherited the industrial development bank with

all its widespread lending power and also the free money policy of our predecessors opposite, who now decry that we are not more generous in our lending, the industrial development bank had 401 loans outstanding totalling $30 million in all.
There was really tight money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Don't these Liberals look sick.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Paul looks like that all the time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Are we going to hear from you?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us look at farm credit. We have heard that subject discussed in the house in the last few days. Legislation has been before the house enlarging the lending power of the Farm Credit Corporation and it can be assumed that as a result of these amendments there will be a further expansion of farm credit lending. I should like to put these figures on the record. The number of farm credit loans made in the three and a half months between July 1 and October 15, 1961 was 2,239. Obviously I have taken October 15 because that is the last date for which we have figures available. During the same period in 1962 these loans increased from 2,239 to 2,808, an increase of almost 600 loans over the same period last year. The amount of these loans for this period last year was $24.9 million and for the same period this year, a tight money period, $34.7 million. I also have the figures for the entire year ended March 31, 1957, just before we came into power. This is a nice little yardstick to look at when comparing generosity with tight money such as we are accused of imposing. In the year ended March 31, 1957 there were only 2,921 loans in all of Canada under the farm loan board and the total amount of these loans was $14 million.
Let us look at export credit financing, which is another phase of credit expansion and development of our economy. The total amount of exports insured in 1961 was $66 million and in 1962 it has increased to $90 million. This gives some indication of the development of our exports, in so far as those receiving financial assistance are concerned.
We have also heard it stated by both hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon that they are worried about unemployment, the fact that unemployment was bound to increase because of the policies which we have followed. I am not minimizing for one minute, Mr. Speaker, the fact that there are some people unemployed in this country. I am not suggesting for one minute that it is
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money not a personal tragedy for anyone who is unemployed. However, this government has done more in trying to overcome the unemployment problem than has any other government. As has been said in the house time and time again during the prior debate and also in public places outside during the summer, employment in 1962 has been about 200,000 higher than in 1961. Since we have come into office over half a million more Canadians are now working than there were before. These people have been provided jobs. Unemployment is continuing to drop. In the last month there were 48,000 fewer unemployed than in the same month last year.
We have had devaluation for a year. We have had tight money for so long. We have had austerity measures. We have had surcharges, and we are told we are faced with doom and disaster.
Well, you created it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If you give us another year in here it will be all over; there will be no unemployment. We created what? The unemployment situation is improving. I must say we are just a little bit weary, a little bored, with having dire prophesies that some terrible thing is going to happen next month or next year. One would think one could get some satisfaction out of improvements. Is jealousy so great in certain places? Is this desire to obtain office so bitter, so biting, so driving in certain places that the record has to be distorted? They hope and pray- they deny that they hope or pray for these things, but let them remember that the prayers of the wicked availeth not. It is rather interesting to note, in view of the prophecies that something bad is going to happen, that they still hope they are wrong. If it is of any comfort to them, I can tell them that they will be wrong.
I should like to leave the question of tight money for a moment because I intend to put some figures on the record at eight o'clock to complete the picture over the period from May and June right down through the rest of this year. I should like to say a word about surcharges for a moment in a general way. The Prime Minister stated when the surcharges were imposed that they were necessary, but they were of a temporary nature and would be removed as soon as it was possible for this to be done. We have already taken some very major steps in that direction. A few weeks ago we removed the surcharges on a large class of goods coming into this country which were used in the production of goods in this country. The government felt
1302	HOUSE OF
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money that to impose surcharges on those goods of a class or kind not made in Canada and used in the production of Canadian goods increased our cost of production to a very substantial degree.
We are dealing with tariff classifications and you cannot deal with every individual item in an individual way as you would like to do. I think it can safely be said, in a general way, that by lifting the surcharges on these items we went a long way toward dealing with those goods of a class or kind not made in Canada and which formed part of our cost of production. I am not going further into the matter at the moment, much as I should like to do so. I regret the fact that the question has been raised here this afternoon. As I said, these matters are under discussion, possibly at the very moment and certainly within the last day or so, and will be again at the GATT negotiations. Our government representatives are there carrying on confidential and detailed discussions with the representatives of the other nations concerning our plans with respect to these surcharges.
I am told that no country has ever before removed charges of this kind so shortly after an exchange crisis. The government is determined to remove these as soon as it is practical or possible to do so. We are not going to remove them at the moment. As I said earlier, we have made a remarkable recovery from the situation with which we were confronted in June. Our exchange reserves have been built up substantially. I noticed an article in a newspaper this morning which suggested that because our exchange reserves are almost as great as they were prior to the crisis, perhaps we would not have to build them up any further. Well, the fact that they were so great a few months ago and faced such a severe run would possibly suggest, or at least some economists would argue, that they should be maintained at an even higher level in the future to make sure, with our expanding trade and our expanding economy, that a similar problem would not arise.
At any rate, the house can rest assured of this, as soon as it is possible, practical and proper so to do, the surcharges are going to be removed. They were and are an essential part of our machinery for safeguarding the Canadian dollar, internally and externally, as we have done. Farther than that, I cannot go on that phase of the situation at the moment.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I think he said there had been a long history of reduction of interest rates.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I said "a steady reduction".
Would the minister care to give some of the figures which might substantiate that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have some here, Mr. Speaker. We have the figures starting in June. The rates went up somewhat in July, with the crisis. In June, on treasury bills for instance, it was 5.45 per cent. In July, it was 5.47 per cent. In August it went down to 4.95 per cent, and in October, it went down to 4.16 per cent.
What was the bank rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The bank rate came down from 6 per cent to 5 per cent during this period. There can be no question but that there has been a reduction in interest rates during this period. As restoration of the reserves made it possible, the Bank of Canada reduced the interest rate with the consent and knowledge of the government and after consulation with the government. The market yields on government of Canada securities are now back to the level at which they stood early in June and so is the spread between long term interest rates in Canada and the United States. I will deal with that matter again for a moment before I sit down. The capital market is receptive to new issues and the confidence of the investing public is demonstrated by the fact that since June 20 they have added a net amount of over $800 million to their holdings of government of Canada securities.
The hon. member for Davenport may be especially interested in this, which affects his own province: only today the province of Ontario has announced a new long term 20-year issue at terms of 5.33 per cent, slightly more favourable than it paid on a similar issue last March, when the percentage was 5.35. That, I should think, coming from the province of Ontario is an indication of the trend. Bank loans have increased substantially. Because of the monetary policy previously followed, the banks were in possession of surplus liquid assets which they were able to sell to meet an expanding loan demand. In September, total general loans of the banks were, on the average, $330 million higher than they were in June and $1,202 million or 22 per cent higher than they were a year ago.
It has been suggested there was a decline in the money supply during the summer. In fact, the impact of this fell on government balances which were high in June. The privately held money supply, which is the only relevant money when it comes to a discussion of "tight money", went on increasing.


In October, the privately held money supply was about $365 million higher than it was in June, an increase as large as one could expect in any such period despite the emergency.
There is clear evidence that the monetary situation has become easier in the last two months. I have already mentioned two examples; I refer to the loans made by the Farm Credit Corporation and others. I want to make it clear, again, that this government is determined to protect the integrity of the Canadian dollar at the present rate of exchange. We are not going to follow policies which result in a fresh devaluation of the Canadian dollar or a fresh loss of confidence in the Canadian dollar. We are convinced that the present exchange rate is a good one for the Canadian economy and that it would help us, along with other measures, to bring our international accounts into closer balances and reduce our dependence on foreign capital. We are convinced that we would be able to follow policies of economic expansion consistently with the protection of the value of the currency and we have already provided evidence that we are determined to move in this direction.
As I said at the outset, the policy of this government is to maintain the integrity of the Canadian dollar, to provide for an expanding economy and at the same time to try to overcome to as substantial an extent as possible the deficit which we are running in current accounts. While this is being done, until we can overcome this deficit-and it cannot be done today or tomorrow-we shall have to be dependent to a certain extent upon the flow of capital from outside this country, and in order to bring that capital here and hold it here there has to be a gap between interest rates here and in the United States, or otherwise there would be an outflow rather than an inflow.
These are the fundamental policies of this government; these are the measures which are attacked in the amendment we have before us. The leader of the New Democratic party asked us this afternoon to bring forth our policies with respect to these matters. Some of those policies we have brought forward. Many of them, as the hon. member knows very well, are budgetary problems which cannot be dealt with at this time. However, I can assure this house that the present government is working on these problems. I have indicated the direction we are taking, and these steps will be followed up by legislative measures and by proposals which will be included in the budget when it is brought down. I am sure the people of Canada generally will wish to co-operate with the government in working toward the solution of

this problem which is one that can be solved by co-operation, understanding and hard work. I know we are on the road to accomplishing this, but it cannot be done by negative amendments such as we have before us at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. T. Asselin (Notre Dame de Grace):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion I have had since becoming a member of this house to offer you my congratulations on your appointment as Speaker. I have had occasion to marvel at your dexterity in dealing even with the most intricate and delicate of procedural problems. To you, and to your deputy, congratulations.
It was 62 years ago that my grandfather the Hon. Senator Edmund William Tobin sat for the first time in this house. The year was 1900. He came to Ottawa to represent the eastern townships' constituency of Richmond-Wolfe. He represented it with devotion and distinction for eight consecutive terms and, needless to say, Mr. Speaker, he was elected under the Liberal banner. He remained in office until June 3, 1930, when he was summoned to the other place. They say that I take after him. I hope so, for at least the next 30 years.
My riding of Notre Dame de Grace is a far cry from my grandfather's rural riding. "NDG", with its 100,000 inhabitants and 60,000 eligible voters, ranks with the country's largest constituencies and closely mirrors the total Canadian ethnic picture. Basically Anglo-Saxon, we have good representation from French-speaking Canadians as well as Canadians of all the other origins which go to make up Canada. Mr. Speaker, when we say the word "Canada" we call to mind a great sweeping panorama that encompasses rugged sea coasts, vast forests, deep flowing rivers, golden prairies, and pure snowcapped mountain peaks. This is fine for the tourist brochures; but for our purpose, for the serious business of government, Canada must be seen as people and problems, for it is its people and problems that are really important.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that more than 65 per cent of all Canadians are now urban dwellers. Sixty five per cent of our countrymen now live in a type of community that the present government has chosen almost to ignore. This is extraordinary, really. What is any country but the sum total of its villages, towns and cities as well as its farms and forests? The economic and sociological health of any urban area extends for many miles beyond its boundaries. It is a major factor in setting the economic pace of the whole nation. The urban problem is not new but it is typical of the problems which Tory austerity measures have made worse. For
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money years now Canadian towns and cities from coast to coast have been seeking assistance for their serious financial and other problems. They have never found the situation so difficult as it has been since the advent of the austerity program. That is the program which the minister denies exists but which anybody can see does exist just by referring for one moment to the submission to the royal commission on banking and finance which was made by every municipality in Canada. The word "austerity" is used there several times, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, used without reference to the high cost of credit to look after their problems.
The Canadian federation of mayors, in their latest brief point out that the urban centres must in large measure "rely on the national economy as a whole for a solution to the needs of urban redevelopment and growth". In all our cities and towns we find a tremendous backlog of unmet demands for social capital, slum clearance, mass transportation, roads to relieve traffic congestion, action on water and air pollution, and the renewal of obsolete and inadequate school facilities-these are among the most important ones. The solution of these problems is important not only to the cities and towns concerned, but it is also vital to the economic growth and development of the nation as a whole. Just because, constitutionally speaking, the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, it becomes too easy for the federal government to shrug off these problems and ignore the fact that many municipal problems present an acute national issue. They are national problems, I repeat, not just because so many of our people are deeply affected, but because they eventually involve our national prosperity in many ways.
Many of these problems started in the early depression years, the early thirties, when residential and municipal construction virtually came to a halt. In the subsequent war years urban problems and needs, including housing, were still relegated to a low priority. After the war, reconstruction and the rapid development of industry, along with the pressures of the Korean war, again forced curtailment of urgent redevelopment in urban areas and strained municipal resources to the limit. In the last few years things should have been different, Mr. Speaker; a new order of national priorities has become necessary.
The need for slum clearance, recreation areas, low cost housing, schools and urban redevelopment generally, confronts us today as urgently as any other national problem. The Canadian people as a whole and their
