Municipal governments should not be backward in pressing their claims on the national economy because they, as urban areas, are responsible for so much of the national economy, an economy, Mr. Speaker, terribly hampered today by Tory austerity or, if you prefer, by tight money policies.
Let us see what the report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment has to say on this point:
We are in a continuing danger of choking our economic growth with congestion, pollution, the development of slums, and with the effects of deficiencies in vital public services and amenities.
Mr. Speaker, that was not a politically biased statement; it was the considered opinion of a group that had carefully studied all aspects of a major national problem and has seen the relationship between urban renewal and the unemployment tragedy. We are faced with a situation today that demands great imagination and effort from federal and provincial authorities if these problems are to be solved. Although the federal government is clearly responsible for the general economic climate of the nation, it has not taken sufficient measures to deal with those particular sources of economic trouble found in urban areas.
There is a great deal of precedent for federal intervention and assistance to municipalities. Take, for example, assistance with regard to slum clearance, low rental housing, hospital construction, removal of level grade railroad crossings, bridges over navigable rivers, sewage disposal, civil defence, vocational and technical training, and the winter works program, although the scale has not been at all adequate, nor has it been planned to give maximum effect. The municipal authorities have said many times that if you strangle traffic you also strangle commerce. Yet so far as the federal government is concerned, it seems that traffic could strangle so completely in our urban centres that the municipalities themselves could wither away. Commerce and industry would disappear also or be obliged to undertake the tremendous expense of relocation and hence become less competitive. However, from the treasury benches in this parliament I have heard no speeches and I have read none from the last one which would indicate the possibility of 

any positive action on this extremely important problem. Basically, the financial resources of most municipalities are heavily committed to the provision of new facilities that expansion demands, such as new sewers, new streets and new lighting. This commitment leaves very little of their revenues available for an attack on the older existing problems. Tremendous population growth has taken place in the last few years and if urban areas had not committed themselves to the cost this growth involves, they and the nation would have ceased to grow. However, a good deal of growth has been at the expense of the commercial hearts of these same cities and towns because money was being spent on new streets and roadways and consequently could not be spent in sufficient amounts for widening old streets, on the construction of expressways or the development of a rapid transit system to handle the movement of people and goods.
Municipal governments must also anticipate continuing growth and development. The volume and nature of foreseeable urban growth and redevelopment within the next ten to 20 years will entail an outlay of social capital that will go far beyond the debt carrying capacity that municipal governments can afford to assume within the framework of their present tax and revenue structures. If the municipalities are to carry out the program required of them and if we are to get this nation's economy moving, we can no longer rely on the government's austerity program. Investment of social capital is necessary in urban areas and it is necessary now. It is necessary to strengthen our national economy.
Together with all members of the official opposition and the representatives of municipalities, large and small, everywhere in Canada, I suggest that a municipal loan bank or fund be created. The government's tight money program has meant increased costs to all Canadians and this includes municipalities. It has restricted the ability of our cities and towns to borrow money and to undertake the backlog of work which is sadly needed and to which I have already referred. A municipal loan fund should be organized in consultation with the provincial and municipal representatives. It will not conflict with existing sources of capital. It will provide loans for sound municipal improvements which, in order to protect their rights, provincial governments would approve but for which capital is unobtainable on reasonable terms from existing Canadian sources.
Loan agencies of this sort have existed in Europe since the 19th century to aid municipalities there. Similar banks or funds exist

in Denmark, Holland, Norway, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Switzerland and Turkey. The United Kingdom's public works loan board is, in many respects, a similar institution. Are we to lag behind Spain and Turkey?
Our party has been advocating a municipal loan fund since 1958. The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, on behalf of large and small municipalities, have been requesting it since 1958. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to think of the force for good it could be. It could provide social capital resulting in schools and low cost housing, but best of all it could provide those things which are so badly needed and which austerity so badly neglects, namely an investment in people and institutions to help people toward a richer and more productive life.
Public requirements have been neglected owing to an outmoded system which places on the municipalities responsibilities far beyond their capacity to assume, without the help of the federal and provincial governments. It is a system which provides the federal government with the bulk of the nation's tax revenue-that is roughly two thirds of the total tax dollar collected from all Canadians-and then makes it difficult, constitutionally speaking, for the federal government to redistribute it where it can be used best. But, Mr. Speaker, just because it is difficult does not mean that we should sit back and, figuratively speaking, twiddle our thumbs as the Conservative government leadership is doing.
A municipal development bank, together with an economic advisory council to plan for a brighter, stronger, expanding economy will be a tremendous force in settling not only major local problems in most of our far flung municipalities from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but also our balance of payments problem and the export-import imbalance. Only long range planning will accomplish this result.
Of course, adequate credit at low interest rates will not solve all of the problems of all of the municipalities in Canada. In depressed areas, in addition to loans the government should make outright grants to municipalities. There are in existence many areas which could be called depressed areas, and I am thinking particularly of those where the economic base has withered away in the Atlantic provinces and in some parts of Quebec and Ontario. Here it will be necessary for the federal government to redistribute tax revenues where they can be used best, not only by means of low cost loans to the municipalities but by means of outright grants

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money Canadian citizens should have received. The hon. member for Laurier has to be thrown out; we have to do away with the chartered banks and replace the present system. Liberals, if you have some cannonballs within your party, the time has come to do away with them, and send them away to sit elsewhere. Please consider the interests of 18 millions of Canadians instead of those of a few bankers who can walk right through your ranks and who will prevent you from ever getting the confidence of the Canadian people. Get rid of that dead wood.
Having spoken with a few of you and with members of other parties, I have come to the conclusion that many of you are sincere and would like nothing better than to improve the state of things in our country. Unfortunately, they are not too sure of what is wrong and they keep on wondering what could be the trouble.
You, Conservatives, Liberals and members of the New Democratic party cannot think straight because your minds are set astray by the so-called financial experts within your ranks who are trying to control your thoughts and to keep you under the present financial system.
Get rid of them. Try to understand that it is the people who must rim the country through their government and not a handful of financiers who want to control Canada's economic and monetary system. Only then, will you be able to see what you can do in such a rich and vast country as Canada.
It will be said that the economists do not share this view. But the economists-and I just happen to see one up there in the gallery; it is the best friend of the hon. member for Laurier, Mr. Lamontagne-and these dear friends, the economists-

I mean the names of the ridings of the hon. members, since we are not allowed to mention them by their own names. However, this was only an example that, to my mind, dealt with the socialists and their planning, and I could not help but name those two individuals. Besides, it was only a comparison.
Reference is often made to the economists, Mr. Speaker. But where have the economists learned their trade? We have some physicians with us in this house who will tell you that after having studied medicine for four or five years, they are sent as resident medical students to a hospital where they learn their trade from practical experience.
After making theoretical studies, a lawyer- and there are many in the house-has to article in a lawyer's office or learn procedure at the court house.
The same thing goes for forestry engineers whom one meets near the forestry engineering building in Quebec city. Every year, in May, you can see them surveying for the nth time the Entente boulevard. Why? To put their theoretical knowledge into practice.
But what have economists learned from practice? They are still studying books dating from 1892 or 1895. They are not aware of what is going on today in our country, on our farms and in our small businesses.
Are you speaking in general?

They are still saying generalities. Let them see what is wrong, in practice, in the country, among the people.
Is it production? Not at all. Some claim that production must be planned. But production is here, and a lot of it. Just call on car dealers and you will see how many cars there are for sale.

Yes indeed.
Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money

Unfortunately, the consumer has no money to buy them.
Call on producers, and you will find that they have products.
But the consumers cannot afford them, they do not have the money to buy the production.
That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. As long as we refuse to tackle this problem-the problem of the consumers who buy the production of their country-as long as we refuse to tackle this particular problem, no workable solution will ever be found. All the solutions that will be brought forward will never help to settle the problem as it should be.
But, Mr. Speaker, let a real investigation be made once and let us regain control over our money and our credit, let us set up a real "debt free money system." When this is done, when we have regained control now in the hands of the chartered banks, we shall-

You agree? All right. If it is so, tell it to your leaders so that they may let you free to express your ideas, let them cease to urge you to share their ideas. Therefore, if you agree, tell them what you think and see to it that means are taken to change the money system that we have now.
Then, when we can control money and credit, we shall be able to put at the consumers' disposal those things that producers can make, and, Mr. Speaker, we shall not have the debt we have now.
A debt-free money system.
That is the first key. And there, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam will not state, with all the candour he can master, that he is in favour of budgetary deficits, even if they mean paying $1,550 million a year in interest.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that the interest paid to the eight chartered banks practically represents all the money taken from our pockets in the form of income tax?
Do you know, Mr. Speaker-

Ask your question.

Tariff Surcharges and Tight Money
Did you ever buy Canada savings bonds?
Yes, I bought some once.
Well, what have you got to say about that?

Yes, that is true, Mr. Speaker. We shall be told that people have bought Canada savings bonds. But I think that the hon. member is not quite aware of what really happens. He should come and see what the worker at the Aluminum Company in Arvida, or at Price Brothers in Kenogami does with those bonds.
At the beginning of the year, he purchases a savings bond of $200 or $500, but when he has finished paying it, if he wants to buy a car or to repair the roof on his house or purchase new furniture, he will cash his bond in a chartered bank, and this is how those banks become holders of all Canada savings bonds. But the workers who buy those bonds have to sell them after a year. This is a fact, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, I purchased a small $100 bond myself and paid it off in a hurry so that I could go to a chartered bank because I was broke.
The worker purchases a savings bond and pays it through pay deductions at the rate of $5 a week. After a year, he cashes his bond to purchase a car, not to pay it entirely, but to make a mere down payment. This is how the Canada savings bonds are used, Mr. Speaker.
Finance companies also hold a great number of victory bonds. Just go and see and you will realize that this is the truth.
That is what 99.9 per cent of the Canadian people are doing. Maybe some members of this house have money enough to keep their bonds, but that is not the case for the majority of the people.
Mr. Speaker, let us set up a debt-free system as outlined in our motion, and on that day, once we have become the masters, we shall control the money in our country. The only way for us to become masters in our country is by controlling the money and the credit in our country.
We shall then see to it that the resources and the abundant and varied production of our country are used to serve our own people. The government can then see to it that enough money is put into circulation to allow the consumer to buy the production instead of remaining an idle victim of production surplusses, as is the case at the present time.


That is the first thing to do, to become the masters of our economy and of our monetary system-a debt-free monetary system.

Then this minister says: Give me another year; give me a chance. Does he wish to raise the rate on these bonds next year up to close to 6 per cent, or another one half of one per cent? There is no doubt that the minister will come out with an optimistic statement. Indeed, I think he has already done so by saying that these bonds would sell well. I think they would sell very well indeed. Why should they not sell well with such a high interest rate? I say it is just another case of mortgaging our future earnings, the wages of the working people, in favour of those people who have money.
I know that a number of people with a small amount of money buy these bonds and it is fine for them. However, many of them do not hold them for very long. I think I heard a previous speaker say-I do not think the case is quite as high-that 99 per cent of them did not hold them over a year or two. I do not know what his percentage was. Certainly the people with more money are holding them a longer time, and the people with no money are trying to pay taxes. That is a point in connection with these bonds.

All this trouble is not recent. I remember something that happened a year ago which I thought was very prophetic. On the very day a year ago when the government was celebrating the fourth anniversary of its accession to power our dollar was falling in the markets of the world and there were no bids on the dollar.
